GC.31.stem: Which of the following is a legal duty required of U.S. citizens, not merely encouraged?

choices.text: Serving on a jury when summoned
Volunteering for a local charity
Following the news on civic issues
Campaigning for a candidate you support

GC.31.reteach: Re-teach the difference between legal duties (obey the law, pay taxes, jury service) and expected-but-optional duties; sort examples into two columns.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Plausible error — volunteering is expected of good citizens but is not legally required.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Plausible error — staying informed is encouraged, not legally compelled.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that civic activity such as campaigning is a legal obligation.

GC.31.key_rationale: Jury service is a legal duty citizens must fulfill when summoned, enforced by the courts.
GC.31.dok_rationale: Recall of a listed fact — sorting a single example as a legal duty.
GC.31.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves which responsibility is a legal requirement.

GC.32.stem: What is the main difference between a primary and a caucus in choosing a party's nominee?

choices.text: A primary is held only in general elections; a caucus only for judges
A primary uses a secret ballot; a caucus uses local meetings and debate
A primary is run by the government; a caucus is illegal in most states
A primary picks a president; a caucus picks a governor

GC.32.reteach: Revisit the nomination funnel: compare primary (ballot vote) and caucus (in-person meeting); re-run the Nominate! simulation.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception about when and for whom each method is used.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that caucuses are illegal or that primaries are government-run rather than party contests.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing the office chosen rather than the method used.

GC.32.key_rationale: A primary selects a nominee by ballot vote, while a caucus selects one through local party meetings and discussion.
GC.32.dok_rationale: Requires comparing two processes on a defining feature, not recalling a single term.
GC.32.blooms_rationale: Student constructs the distinction between two nomination methods.

GC.33.stem: How can the wording of a public-opinion poll question affect the results it produces?

choices.text: Wording cannot change results because opinions are fixed before the poll
Only the number of people surveyed affects results, never the wording
Leading or loaded wording can push respondents toward a particular answer
Poll results are always accurate no matter how questions are worded

GC.33.reteach: Reread the poll-wording example; have students rewrite a neutral question as a leading one and predict the shift.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that public opinion is fixed and unaffected by measurement.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Partial evidence — sample size matters, but wording is overlooked.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that polls are objective regardless of question design.

GC.33.key_rationale: Leading or loaded wording can nudge respondents toward a particular answer, so question design shapes the result.
GC.33.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing how question design influences data, not recalling a definition.
GC.33.blooms_rationale: Student breaks apart how framing affects measured opinion.

GC.34.stem: Which First Amendment protections most directly allow citizens to march in a protest and sign a petition?

choices.text: The rights to bear arms and to a jury trial
The rights to due process and equal protection
The rights against self-incrimination and unreasonable search
The rights to peaceably assemble and to petition the government

GC.34.reteach: Reread Amendment I; underline 'assemble' and 'petition' and connect each to a real form of participation.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error citing Second and Sixth Amendment rights.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error citing Fourteenth Amendment protections.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error citing Fifth and Fourth Amendment rights.

GC.34.key_rationale: The First Amendment protects the rights to peaceably assemble and to petition the government, the direct basis for protest and petition.
GC.34.dok_rationale: Requires matching a constitutional protection to civic actions, beyond simple recall.
GC.34.blooms_rationale: Student explains which rights enable specific participation.

formA.stem: Thomas Jefferson wrote that 'wherever the people are well informed they can be trusted with their own government.' Which civic responsibility does this statement most directly support?

choices.text: Paying federal income taxes on time
Serving in the armed forces when called
Staying informed on civic issues
Obeying local traffic laws

formA.reteach: Reread Jefferson's letter to Richard Price; tie 'well informed' to the responsibility of staying informed.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Partial evidence — a real duty, but not the one Jefferson's statement addresses.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Partial evidence — a valid responsibility unrelated to being informed.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Partial evidence — a legal duty, but not what the quotation supports.

formA.key_rationale: Jefferson ties safe self-government to an informed public, directly supporting the responsibility to stay informed.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires interpreting a primary source to identify the responsibility it supports.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student infers a responsibility from Jefferson's reasoning.

formA.stem: In the presidential nomination process, what is the purpose of the primaries and caucuses held state by state?

choices.text: To choose each party's nominee before the general election
To count the electoral votes after the general election
To confirm the President's cabinet appointments
To redraw congressional district boundaries

formA.reteach: Trace the path primary/caucus → convention → general election; label what each step decides.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing nomination with the Electoral College count.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing nomination with Senate confirmation.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing elections with redistricting.

formA.key_rationale: State primaries and caucuses select each party's nominee before the general election.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the function of a stage in the process, not naming a term.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student explains the purpose of the nomination stage.

formA.stem: A news outlet covers one issue heavily every night for a week while barely mentioning others. How does this most likely influence the public?

choices.text: It guarantees the public will oppose the government entirely
It has no effect, since the public ignores repeated stories
It forces rival outlets to drop the issue completely
It makes the issue seem more important than others

formA.reteach: Reteach agenda-setting: the media shapes which issues seem to matter; find a current example of heavy vs. light coverage.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Overgeneralization — coverage does not dictate a single public reaction.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that repeated coverage has no agenda-setting effect.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — one outlet's focus does not control competitors.

formA.key_rationale: Heavy, repeated coverage raises an issue's perceived importance, the agenda-setting effect.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing the effect of coverage patterns on public priorities.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes how coverage shapes perceived importance.

formA.stem: Which action gives citizens a way to directly propose or overturn a law themselves, rather than only influencing officials?

choices.text: Campaigning for a candidate who supports the law
Using an initiative or referendum
Lobbying a legislator to sponsor a bill
Writing a letter to a representative

formA.reteach: Contrast direct democracy (initiative, referendum, recall) with indirect influence (lobbying, campaigning); sort each example.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — a real form of participation, but it influences officials rather than making law directly.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — lobbying pressures officials rather than letting voters act directly.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — contacting a representative is indirect influence, not direct lawmaking.

formA.key_rationale: Initiative and referendum are direct-democracy tools that let voters propose or reject a law themselves.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires distinguishing direct-democracy tools from indirect influence.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student differentiates direct action from influencing officials.

formB.stem: A citizen who is called for jury service is fulfilling a responsibility that is best described as:

choices.text: entirely optional for everyone
required only of public officials
limited to voters over age 35
a legal duty the courts enforce

formB.reteach: Reteach jury service as a legal duty tied to the 6th and 7th Amendments; list who can be summoned.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that jury service is optional.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that the duty applies only to officials.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception adding an age limit that does not define the duty.

formB.key_rationale: Jury service is a legal responsibility that citizens must meet when summoned, enforced by the courts.
formB.dok_rationale: Recall of the nature of a listed responsibility.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student retrieves that jury service is a legal duty.

formB.stem: George Washington warned against 'the spirit of party,' yet political parties quickly became central to elections. What role do parties play in the political system?

choices.text: They write the amendments to the U.S. Constitution
They serve as the nation's court system
They organize voters and nominate candidates for office
They command the national armed forces

formB.reteach: Revisit Washington's Farewell Address and the rise of parties; list what parties actually do in elections.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing parties with the Article V amendment process.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing parties with the judicial branch.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error confusing parties with the executive military role.

formB.key_rationale: Political parties organize voters and nominate candidates, structuring how elections work.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the function of parties, not recalling a single fact.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student explains the role parties play in elections.

formB.stem: Two newspapers report the same city council vote. One headline reads 'Council Protects Taxpayers'; the other reads 'Council Cuts Vital Services.' What does this best illustrate?

choices.text: Media framing can shape how the public feels about the same event
One newspaper reported false information about the vote
The city council changed its decision between the reports
Headlines have no measurable effect on public opinion

formB.reteach: Reteach framing vs. bias vs. falsehood; have students reframe one neutral headline two opposite ways.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Causal attribution error — different framing is not the same as false reporting.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that differing headlines mean the underlying event changed.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception that framing has no effect on opinion.

formB.key_rationale: Two opposite headlines for one event show that framing shapes public perception without changing the facts.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing how framing produces different impressions of one event.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes the effect of framing on opinion.

formB.stem: A citizen meets with a state legislator to try to persuade the legislator to support a new bill. This form of participation is called:

choices.text: petitioning
lobbying
demonstrating
running for office

formB.reteach: Reteach the vocabulary of participation; match each scenario to campaigning, demonstrating, lobbying, petitioning, or running for office.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — petitioning is a written request signed by many, not a one-on-one persuasion meeting.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — demonstrating is public protest, not private persuasion of an official.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — running for office is seeking a seat, not persuading a sitting legislator.

formB.key_rationale: Trying to influence an official's decision is lobbying.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires classifying a scenario under the correct participation term.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student applies a participation category to a scenario.

_psychometric_summary.note: IRT 3PL parameters are pre-field-test design-time estimates, to be calibrated on field-test data.
